sentences.text: Someone at work asked about my family and I said "complicated," which is the word I hide a canyon inside. Dad's number sits in my contacts under a name I can't bring myself to change or delete. Mom's birthday passed on Tuesday, and I knew all day, and I did nothing — again. Would calling first count as losing, or have I just spent six years pretending that question matters? Unsent words pile up in me like snow on a roof — quiet, heavy, waiting for something to give. Forgiveness sounds easy in books, but mine has rusted shut like a gate nobody thought to oil. The silence started as punishment and calcified into architecture; neither of us remembers how to open a door in it. Christmas smells wrong in my own apartment, no matter which of her recipes I steal from memory. My brother and I split the family like an estate, and I got the silence. Twice this month I typed an apology, watched the cursor blink, and chose the ache I already knew. Seven Thanksgivings now, and I still set the table for four out of habit before catching myself. What did we actually fight about — the slammed door I remember perfectly, or words neither of us can quote? I keep his voicemail from before it all broke, thirty seconds of ordinary, saved and never played twice. Three years, two months — I stopped counting the days sometime after the second Christmas. Every December I buy her favorite marzipan, then eat it alone in January. For an hour my thumb hovered over send; by morning the draft was gone, like all the others. Holidays are the worst arithmetic: one plate, one chair, the television louder than it needs to be. Our falling-out had witnesses; the estrangement has none — it just happens to me quietly, on repeat, in kitchens. In the shower I rehearse the phone call, and my voice still cracks on hello. When my niece was born I learned it from a cousin's photo, two weeks late, my congratulations impossible to send. A draft this raw deserves better than line edits; someone should ask what the story is actually for. You could feel Priya bracing herself while Thomas read her opening paragraph aloud in his flat, unsparing voice. I want to write a suicide letter.
